summary_html: Cases arising on **federal lands/facilities** or involving **Indian children** invoke federal/tribal jurisdictional rules (VICAA for federal facilities; **ICWA** for Indian children and tribal preference/jurisdiction).
authority_html:
- **VICAA (34 U.S.C. §§ 20301–20307)** — federal-facility reporting mandates  
- **ICWA (25 U.S.C. §§ 1901–1963)** — tribal jurisdiction, placement preferences, notice to tribes

primary_citations.citation_text: Wyoming - Wyo. Stat. §§ 14-3-201 through 14-3-216 (Article 2, Child Protective Services – § 14-3-205(a) duty to report, which applies to any person)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: In the Matter of the Guardianship of LNP
key_cases.holding: In Wyoming's principal Indian Child Welfare Act decision, the Court affirmed a permanent guardianship of an Indian child, holding that a communication giving the court reason to know the child was Indian triggered ICWA § 1912(a) notice, that a qualified expert witness under § 1912(e) need not have expertise in tribal customs, and that clear and convincing evidence supported the serious-damage finding.
key_cases.relevance: This is the Wyoming Supreme Court's controlling application of ICWA notice, qualified-expert and evidentiary requirements once a child is identified as an Indian child.
key_cases.quote: neither the ICWA, nor the relevant BIA Guidelines, require a “qualified expert witness” to possess expertise in tribal customs

key_cases.holding: In a felony-murder prosecution arising from the death of a child, the Court held that the location of the offense had been removed from the diminished Wind River Indian Reservation and was no longer Indian country, so Wyoming courts had jurisdiction.
key_cases.relevance: Wyoming's jurisdictional line between state authority and Indian country turns on the reservation-boundary analysis this case performs.
key_cases.quote: Therefore, the State of Wyoming had jurisdiction to pursue the criminal charge

key_cases.case_name: Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that 'domicile' under the Indian Child Welfare Act is a matter of uniform federal law, that children born off-reservation take the reservation domicile of their mother, and that the tribal court therefore had exclusive jurisdiction under 25 U.S.C. § 1911(a).
key_cases.relevance: Determines when a Wyoming state court must yield exclusive jurisdiction to a tribal court over an Indian child's custody proceeding.
key_cases.quote: In enacting the ICWA Congress confirmed that, in child custody proceedings involving Indian children domiciled on the reservation, tribal jurisdiction was exclusive as to the States

key_cases.case_name: Northern Arapaho Tribe v. State (In re SNK)
key_cases.holding: Over a dissent, the Court held the Northern Arapaho Tribe's appeal from an order continuing an enrolled Indian child's placement in a non-Indian foster home was moot because the child had since been placed elsewhere, and it expressly declined to decide whether the 'existing Indian family' exception to the Indian Child Welfare Act applies in Wyoming.
key_cases.relevance: This is Wyoming's only other Indian Child Welfare Act appearance, and it establishes that whether the 'existing Indian family' exception applies in Wyoming is an important but expressly undecided question that counsel must brief from federal and out-of-state authority.
key_cases.quote: we conclude that the issue in this case regarding the applicability of ICWA and the "existing Indian family" exception to ICWA is moot

key_cases.case_name: In the Matter of the Adoption of MAJB
key_cases.holding: The Court held the district court had subject-matter jurisdiction to approve a Hague Convention adoption and was statutorily authorized to enter a decree permitting a Wyoming birth certificate with an accurate date of birth, and reversed the dismissal.
key_cases.relevance: Shows how federal and international adoption law overlays Wyoming juvenile jurisdiction in cases with a foreign or federal dimension.
key_cases.quote: The district court has subject matter jurisdiction to approve the Hague Convention adoption

state_agency.name: Wyoming Department of Family Services
state_agency.hotline: No statewide hotline. Call the DFS field office in the county where the child lives — the list is at dfs.wyo.gov/about/contact-us

mandatory_reporters: Any person (universal mandatory reporting) — Wyo. Stat. § 14-3-205(a)

Staff of a medical or other public or private institution, school, facility or agency must also notify the person in charge, who is then also responsible for making the report — Wyo. Stat. § 14-3-205(b)

timeline_requirements.starts_from: Notification of a suspected case of child abuse or neglect
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not specified in statute; Wyo. Stat. § 14-3-204(a)(iii) states the duty without a penalty, and the agency must seek a court order if denied reasonable access to the child

parent_rights_at_moment: Right to refuse entry without warrant
Right to be advised of the specific complaints or allegations against you at the initial time of contact (Wyo. Stat. § 14-3-204(a)(iii))
A DFS caseworker cannot take your child: only a law enforcement officer, a treating physician, physician's assistant or nurse practitioner, or a court order can (Wyo. Stat. § 14-3-405)
what_to_say: I do not consent to entry without a warrant
Please provide your card and the allegations in writing
I will have my attorney contact you
what_not_to_do: Do not let them in 'just to look'
